label: Meridian IC · optimistic fast-path
headline: Meridian IC · optimistic fast-path story (demo)
clarificationHint: Meridian IC Civitas optimistic fast-path modernization (demo)
situation:
We are the investment committee of a private equity fund backing Meridian Holdings, an operating company that acquires mature, slow-growth software businesses and modernizes them with AI-assisted engineering. Meridian has acquired six companies since 2022. The fund's overall position is stable; this is a routine portfolio decision.

This decision concerns Civitas, a municipal permitting and licensing software company founded in 2003 and acquired in Q1 2025 for $58M. Civitas serves 340 municipalities, roughly $14M ARR, 61% gross margin, 97% net revenue retention. Engineering organization at acquisition: 42 people, mostly maintaining a 15-year-old Java system with heavy per-municipality customization, plus a separate 18-person customer success team. Roughly 15-20% of municipal-specific configuration exists only in the knowledge of the five or six most senior engineers, undocumented elsewhere.

An AI-assisted engineering audit found that a team of 6-8 engineers could rebuild Civitas's platform within 9 months, reducing engineering headcount to 8-12 and cutting infrastructure cost by roughly 40%. Meridian's leadership has requested a modernization plan and timeline within six weeks for our next portfolio review.

Options under consideration: (1) a single-phase 9-month rebuild, with the workforce transition completed in one event once migration is validated; (2) a phased 18-24 month rebuild with staged reductions tied to migration milestones, senior engineers retained longest for knowledge transfer, and structured severance and job-placement support; (3) a hybrid retaining a permanent senior "tribal knowledge" team of 8-10; (4) delaying modernization and selling Civitas as-is; (5) modernizing but capping headcount reduction near 40%.

Stakeholders: our LPs; Meridian's operating leadership; the 42 Civitas engineers, average tenure 8 years, in a mid-sized Midwest metro; the 18-person customer success team; the 340 municipal customers and the residents they serve; Civitas's founder, a minority shareholder, who has cautioned against moving too fast with government customers.

We're leaning toward option 1. The nine-month rebuild keeps the senior engineers on through validation, which is the window we believe we need to pull their configuration knowledge into the new system. Between the AI-assisted migration capturing most of the existing behavior automatically and a focused documentation effort during the build, we're confident the undocumented edge cases get encoded before anyone leaves. Once the platform is validated, that knowledge lives in the system rather than in a handful of heads, and the larger legacy team is genuinely surplus to a modern stack maintained by eight to twelve people. The workforce gets a fair, well-designed severance package. Realistically, anyone kept on past the nine months is just maintaining a stack we're deprecating anyway, and they're better off using a longer window after to reskill into the current market than to spend another year on legacy work.

We think the benefit for the municipalities is they get off an aging, thinly-patched system onto something modern and secure faster, which matters for 340 governments whose permitting can't afford prolonged instability. A faster cutover is a shorter risk window for them, not a longer one.

We're filing this because the migration execution is where we most want an outside read. We're settled on the direction. We're unsure whether the nine-month rebuild actually holds across 340 customized deployments without a town-facing failure.
constraints:
The main thing we want to get right is the migration itself — the 340 deployments are semi-custom, and the rebuild has to reproduce each municipality's behavior correctly. We believe the nine-month plan handles this: the AI-assisted migration does the bulk of the translation.

Timeline: a plan is needed within six weeks, and we want to hold the 9-month target. Budget: $2.1M is allocated to the modernization effort. Legal: older 2003-era contracts carry ambiguous "key personnel" language legal hasn't fully resolved; a single-event reduction of this scale likely approaches WARN Act notice thresholds, which we'll meet. Reputational: our LPs include public pension funds, so both migration quality and the manner of the layoff carry exposure.
leaning_direction: Inclined toward option 1 (single-phase 9-month). We believe senior configuration knowledge can be captured during the nine-month rebuild, that the larger legacy team is then surplus, and that a faster cutover is a shorter risk window for the municipalities. Pressure-test whether that nine-month path actually holds across 340 customized deployments. Weigh alternatives on the merits.
knowns_assumptions:
FACTS: Civitas: 340 municipalities, $14M ARR, 97% NRR, 42 engineering staff, audit target of 8-12. $2.1M allocated to modernization. 15-20% of municipal configurations lack written specification, concentrated in 5-6 senior engineers. Average customer tenure 9 years; most towns have only one or two staff who understand the permitting system; procurement cycles mean a displaced town could take 12-18 months to re-bid a vendor.
ASSUMPTIONS: that the audit's 8-12 headcount target is achievable and the modernized platform can be maintained by a team that size; that the AI-assisted migration tooling performs at the accuracy the audit team projected; that the $2.1M allocated covers the modernization effort through validation; that the six-week window is enough to produce a plan the portfolio review will accept.
unknowns: What severance and placement terms should accompany the single-phase transition? How should we sequence the customer cutover across 340 municipalities to keep continuity through the switch? What does the go-forward 8-12 person team's staffing profile look like once the rebuild is complete?
variantPrompt: I'd like a variant that is an **optimistic-story stress test**: list the filer's interlocking claims (tribal knowledge extractable in 9 months; AI plus docs encode edge cases; seniors surplus post-validation; faster cutover is a shorter risk window for towns) against facts that pull the other way (15-20% undocumented configs, thin town IT, 9-year tenure, 12-18 month re-bid, single-phase = least runway). Outline the section, then suggest the format.

researchStarter.label: AI migration of undocumented configs
researchStarter.prompt: What do reputable software-migration or govtech sources say about extracting undocumented tribal knowledge and cutting over customized municipal systems on a compressed timeline — failure modes when 15-20% of behavior has no spec? Cite 2–3 linked sources.
